summary: An announcement from BBN of a planned release of IMPSYS 2600, a major new IMP program, for May 15, 1972. It would be tried on an experimental basis and the older IMPSYS 2514 reloaded if problems occurred. Sites were asked to help load a new tape and avoid scheduling production work during the switchover. It was replaced by RFC 343.

plainLanguage.summary: The people who run the network's traffic machines said they would swap in new software on one day. They asked everyone to help and not to plan important work then, in case it went wrong.

questions: how was the new imp software rolled out
how did the arpanet upgrade software
subtitle: Planning a major upgrade to the ARPANET's packet routers

tldr.problem: The ARPANET's IMP (Interface Message Processor) software was ready for a major update that would change how packets were routed and tracked, but the change was risky and could disrupt the network.
tldr.mechanism: BBN announced it would release IMPSYS 2600 on May 15, 1972, replacing the current system IMPSYS 2514. It asked each ARPANET site to help load new tapes and prepared to revert to the old system if problems appeared.
tldr.outcome: The release proceeded on an experimental basis. If failures occurred, the old system would be reloaded. Hosts would see no first-order effects because message formats were unchanged, but the statistics package was heavily modified.

today: RFC 331 describes a critical software upgrade on the early ARPANET. This RFC was superseded by RFC 343, which provided updated information about the IMPSYS 2600 release. The upgrade was part of the continuous evolution of ARPANET infrastructure in its first years of operation.

sections.title: The IMPSYS 2600 Release
sections.content: On April 19, 1972, Jim McQuillan of BBN announced that IMPSYS 2600, a major upgrade to the IMP (Interface Message Processor) software, would be released on May 15, 1972, between noon and 3 p.m. EDT. This constituted a major change to the core routing software of every IMP on the ARPANET. Because of the magnitude of the change, the system would be released on an experimental basis: if problems appeared, the current system (IMPSYS 2514) would be reloaded and the cutover would be rescheduled for a later time.
sections.plainLanguage: BBN said it would swap the software in the network's traffic routers on a specific day. If things went wrong, they could switch back.

sections.title: What Sites Had to Do
sections.content: The switchover required assistance from personnel at each ARPANET site. BBN would mail a new IMPLOD 2600 tape to each site and call them on May 15 to load it and follow detailed procedures. BBN preferred to have on-site personnel familiar with IMP operations present. In case of serious problems, BBN might request assistance from site computer operations staff or programmers. All sites were advised to refrain from scheduling production network traffic during the switchover window due to the risk of unforeseen difficulties.
sections.plainLanguage: Each site got a new tape in the mail and had to put it in their machine when BBN called. People were told not to plan important work that day.

sections.title: What Would Change and What Wouldn't
sections.content: The announcement emphasized that hosts would not see first-order effects from the switchover because leader formats and message types were not changed. However, the statistics package had been extensively modified, and the Network Measurement Center was notified of these changes. Additionally, the Very Distant Host option would be included in IMPSYS 2600 and was expected to be activated for use around June 1, 1972. Detailed technical changes would be described in a forthcoming revision to BBN Report 1822, the standard reference for IMP behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The way computers talked to the routers didn't change, so they didn't need new code. But the routers would keep track of their work differently, and could soon talk to computers very far away.
